Baseline diagnosis - Build an evidence-based baseline before benefits forecasts 3 DATA TO COLLECT Population, income, car availability, employment, schools, O–D patterns, traffic counts, existing buses and observed travel times. Existing TRANSPORT PERFORMANCE Level of service (LOS); volume/capacity (V/C); VKT/VMT; VHT; peak hr traffic delays; existing public transport ridership and bus boardings and passenger crowding (peak/off-peak). BASE-YEAR MODEL CALIBRATION & VALIDATION – CRITICAL Calibration: Adjust model parameters using observed traffic counts, screenline flows, bus boardings & travel times. Validation: Compare model predictions against actual observed transport conditions to assess accuracy. Example: If the model predicts 5,000 vehicles/hr. crossing a screenline towards the CBD, compare it with actual traffic counts. Outcome: Model predictions must be validated against real-world data before forecasting metro benefits.

Trip generation Households, jobs and trip purpose → Trip productions and attractions → 2. Trip distribution Suburb–CBD and intermediate destinations → O–D trip tables → 3. Mode choice Car, metro, bus, walk/cycle, P&R → mode split (%) → 4. Assignment Assign trips to road and public transport networks → forecast road traffic volumes and metro station passenger demand P&R - For 25 km metro corridor: Passengers drive to a metro station, park their cars, and take the metro to the CBD. ITERATE: congested travel times from assignment feed back into destination and mode choices.

Four-step travel-demand forecasting - A practical model chain for the metro, feeder buses and competing roads 2 ITERATION - Repeating the travel-demand modelling process until the predictions are consistent and reliable. Example for your 25 km metro corridor: Initial prediction: Car travel from suburbs to CBD takes 30 minutes. Network assignment: The model identifies congestion, increasing travel time to 50 minutes. Feedback: The increased travel time may encourage passengers to switch from cars to metro or choose different destinations. Recalculate: The model updates traffic volumes, mode split and travel times. Purpose: Ensure the model reflects realistic traffic congestion and passenger travel choices.

Corridor modelling & Mode choice 5 CORRIDOR PLANNING Fine traffic analysis zones (TAZs), detailed access links and AM/PM peak plus off-peak trip patterns; 20–30 year land-use scenarios. TRAVEL TIME AND COST Compare door-to-door time: access, waiting, in-vehicle and transfer time; fares, parking cost, comfort and reliability. POLICY PLANNING AND ANALYSIS Test fare and parking prices, service frequency, household and job growth, CBD policies and whether promised TOD is delivered. Use a calibrated four-step model first; add detailed simulations where station or junction operations demand it. Example for 25 km metro corridor: Divide suburban residential areas into smaller zones. Identify population, households, employment and trips generated in each zone. Estimate travel demand from each zone to metro stations and the CBD. Purpose: Improve the accuracy of ridership forecasts, station locations and feeder bus planning.

Integrated metro, feeder buses & park-and-ride 6 METRO – MAIN TRANSIT CORRIDOR Reliable high-capacity service between suburbs, intermediate activity centres and the CBD. FEEDER BUS – FIRST- AND LAST-MILE CONNECTIVITY Provide feeder bus connections to metro stations, reduce waiting and transfer times, and improve accessibility from surrounding residential and commercial areas. PARK & RIDE – METRO STATION ACCESS Provide appropriately located and priced park-and-ride facilities at metro stations to improve accessibility, encourage transfers from private cars to metro, and reduce car traffic towards the CBD. Evaluate total door-to-door travel time, including walking, waiting, in-vehicle travel and transfer time, rather than metro travel speed alone

Transit-oriented development (TOD) at four stations Use the four Ds of the built environment; design for accessibility, not density alone. 7 DENSITY Promote higher residential and employment density around metro stations. DIVERSITY Promote mixed-use development, including residential, commercial, offices and community services around metro stations. DESIGN Provide safe pedestrian crossings, walkable streets, continuous sidewalks and universal accessibility around metro stations. DESTINATIONS Improve connectivity and accessibility to employment, education, shopping and essential services through metro stations. Promote affordable, accessible and mixed-use development around metro stations to increase public transport ridership and reduce car dependency.

Road Management, Nonmotorized Transport & Policy Planning 8 ROAD / PARKING POLICY Test junction management, bus priority, pricing of CBD parking and, only if suitable, cordon/congestion pricing or HOV/HOT options. WALKING & CYCLING Provide continuous station access, safe crossings, cycle parking, inclusive design, lighting and passenger security. CAUTION More road capacity or abundant free station parking does not necessarily create more accessibility. Evaluate person movement, safety and land opportunity cost. For 25 km metro corridor, nonmotorized transport is important for first- and last-mile connectivity, allowing passengers to walk or cycle to metro stations

Major Trends in Travel Demand Modeling • Four-step models have been enhanced through time-of-day analysis, vehicle availability, nonmotorized travel, and improved component specifications. • GPS and improved household, transit-rider, and traffic-count surveys have strengthened travel-data collection. • Travel-demand software increasingly integrates with GIS and modern computing environments. • Integrated land use–transportation modeling has expanded beyond static land- use allocation. • Tour/activity-based approaches and integration with traffic simulation represent major methodological advances. 5

Changing Planning Questions • Models now support analysis of toll roads, HOT lanes, cordon pricing, and time-varying congestion pricing. • They are used to examine alternative land-use patterns and their influence on travel demand. • Environmental applications include climate impacts, energy use, emissions, and air quality. • Traditional uses remain central: long-range plans, highway/transit project evaluation, air-quality conformity, and site-impact studies. • Model structure and complexity should therefore be aligned with the planning question being investigated. 6

1.3 Conventional Four-Step Travel Modeling Framework A sequential analytical representation of travel demand—not a literal sequence of human decision making 1 Trip Generation Productions & attractions 2 Trip Distribution Origin–destination pattern 3 Mode Choice Trips by travel mode 4 Assignment Network loading Critical point: Destination, mode, and other travel decisions may be simultaneous and interdependent. The four-step sequence is a computational simplification used for planning analysis. 7

Step 1 — Trip Generation: Analytical Interpretation • Purpose: estimate the number of trips produced and attracted by each geographic unit, commonly a Traffic Analysis Zone (TAZ). • Trips are segmented by purpose because travel behavior varies by purpose; the report identifies home-based work, home-based nonwork, and nonhome-based as the 'classic three'. • Typical explanatory variables include household size, workers, vehicle availability, income, and employment by type. • Outputs are productions and attractions by zone and purpose; these become the demand totals used in trip distribution. • Key modeling question: are the selected explanatory variables behaviorally meaningful and supported by available data? 8

Step 2 — Trip Distribution: Spatial Interaction • Trip distribution connects the productions and attractions estimated during trip generation. • It estimates how many trips occur between origins and destinations, producing zonal trip tables by purpose. • Travel impedance—especially travel time/cost between zones—is a central explanatory element. • Destination attractiveness and origin activity also influence the spatial pattern of trips. • Because travel times can change after assignment, distribution may be affected by feedback from later model stages. 9

Step 3 — Mode Choice: Representing Modal Decisions • Mode choice divides distributed person trips among the transportation options represented in the model. • Broad categories include automobile, transit, and nonmotorized modes; transit can be segmented by access and service type. • Auto alternatives may be distinguished by vehicle occupancy. • Outputs include person-trip tables by mode/purpose and vehicle-trip tables required for highway assignment. • Model specification must reflect the alternatives actually available to travelers and the policy questions being tested. 10

Step 4 — Assignment: Loading Demand onto Networks • Highway assignment routes vehicle O–D demand onto network paths and produces link volumes, speeds, and travel times. • Transit assignment loads transit trip tables onto routes and links and produces route volumes plus station/stop boardings and alightings. • Assignment connects modeled demand with network performance and congestion. • Travel times generated at this stage can influence earlier demand-model components, motivating iterative feedback. 11

Supporting Components of the Model Chain • Time-of-day modeling divides daily demand into periods such as AM peak, PM peak, midday, and evening. • External travel models represent trips crossing the model-area cordon. • Freight/commercial vehicle travel is significant and is better represented through separate truck/commercial trip tables than by simple passenger-trip factors. • Vehicle availability and automobile occupancy may also be represented as supplementary model components. • These additions improve the behavioral and operational realism of the basic four- step framework. 12

1.6 Emerging and Advanced Modeling Practices • Conventional four-step procedures -- rapid advances in travel modeling. • Activity-based models represent travel through linked activities and travel patterns rather than treating each trip as fully independent. • Dynamic traffic assignment introduces time-varying network conditions and route- choice interactions. • Traffic simulation provides more detailed representation of network operations. • These methods are extensions/alternatives whose structure differs from conventional aggregate models. 17

Four-Step vs. Emerging Approaches — Discussion Framework • Unit of analysis: individual trips in the conventional framework versus richer activity/tour representations in advanced approaches. • Temporal representation: daily or period-based demand versus more explicit time- dependent behavior. • Network interaction: static/sequential representation versus stronger dynamic interaction in simulation. • Data and computational needs generally increase as behavioral and operational detail increases. • The appropriate approach depends on the planning application, available data, resources, and required analytical resolution. 18

Critical Thinking Exercise • A city has limited household-travel survey data but wants to develop a four-step model. Which model parameters could reasonably be transferred, and what evidence would you require before using them? • If assignment produces much longer congested travel times than those used in trip distribution and mode choice, what modeling problem arises and how should it be addressed? • How would the modeling requirements differ for: (a) a 25-year regional plan, (b) a new metro corridor, and (c) congestion pricing? • Under what circumstances would an activity-based or dynamic model provide enough additional value to justify its greater data and computational requirements? 21

Transportation Problems Service-related issues: Poor or unreliable transport service, such as delays, low frequency, or uncomfortable vehicles. Congestion: Too many vehicles use the road at the same time, causing slow traffic and delays. Inadequate capacity: Roads or public transport systems cannot handle the amount of traffic or passengers. Higher user costs: Travelers spend more on fuel, fares, parking, maintenance, and travel time. Safety issues: More traffic can increase the risk of crashes, injuries, and unsafe conditions. Right-of-way and relocation issues: New roads may require land acquisition and sometimes relocation of homes or businesses. Air pollution: Vehicles release harmful gases and particles that reduce air quality. Noise: Heavy traffic produces unwanted sound that affects nearby residents.

Goals related to transportation service, impact and affecting factors are: Increased access Efficiency and Economy Conservation of natural resources Performance measures Travel times Constraints and Standards Budget Transportation Goals and Objectives

Transportation Goals and Objectives Increased access: Provide people with easier access to jobs, schools, hospitals, markets, and other important places. Efficiency and economy: Move people and goods in a way that saves time, fuel, and money. Conservation of natural resources: Reduce unnecessary use of fuel, land, and other resources, and encourage sustainable transport. Performance measures: Use indicators such as speed, delay, congestion, safety, and reliability to check how well the transport system is working. Travel times: Reduce the time people spend travelling and make trips more predictable. Constraints and standards: Transportation projects must follow design standards, safety rules, environmental requirements, and available space limitations. Budget: Plans must be developed within the available financial resources and should provide the best possible benefit for the cost.

Short term transportation planning : Intended for projects implemented in 1 to 3 years to provide better management of existing facilities e.g Traffic signal retiming, transit improvements. Long term transportation planning Considers projects to be constructed over a 20 year period .Adding new highway elements, adding bus lines or freeway lanes, etc. Transportation Planning-Time Horizons

A system descriptive model is a simple representation that shows the main parts of a system, how they are connected, and what each part does. In transportation planning, a road network can be treated as a system in which intersections are the main components and road links connect these components. Traffic entering and leaving each intersection must follow the principle of flow conservation, meaning that the total traffic entering an intersection should equal the total traffic leaving it. TRANSPORTATION PLANNING AND ENGINEERING TE-501A Introduction Lecture # 1 Dr. Hina Saleemi Assistant Professor Department of Transportation Engineering & Management University of Engineering & Technology, Lahore 1

To provide comprehensive theoretical and technical knowledge of the concepts involved in Transportation Planning and Engineering along with the analytical tools and methodologies that are used in practical application. Course Objectives

Transportation Planning related topics are intended to provide knowledge of different planning principles, relationship between transportation and land use, travel demand forecasting, demand versus supply characteristics, and the development and evaluation of alternative systems. Transportation Engineering related topics will cover design and operation of transportation systems as well as strategies to improve system efficiency and safety. Course Objectives

This course is intended to provide students with in depth theoretical and technical knowledge of Transportation Planning and Engineering concepts as well as prepare them for the practical tasks involved in planning, design and operation of the transportation system and developing strategies to improve the system efficiency and safety. Course Outcomes

• Transportation Planning • Transportation Engineering • What planning is About? • What is Transportation means? • Transportation System • Transportation system Classification • Transportation Planning Outcomes • Transportation Project • Factors Affecting Transportation Projects Lecture Outline

What is Transportation Planning?  Planning is done by human beings for human beings. It is future oriented and optimistic.  Urban Transportation Planning (TP) is the process that leads to decision on transportation policies and programs. The objective of TP process is to provide information necessary for making decisions on when and where improvements should be made in the transportation system, thus promoting travel and land development patterns that are in keeping with community goals and objectives.

An Overview Of Transportation Planning  Monitoring existing conditions;  Forecasting future population and employment growth, including assessing projected land uses in the region and identifying major growth corridors;  Identifying current and projected future transportation problems and needs and analyzing, through detailed planning studies, various transportation improvement strategies to address those needs;  Developing long-range plans and short-range programs of alternative capital improvement and operational strategies for moving people and goods;  Estimating the impact of recommended future improvements to the transportation system on environmental features, including air quality; and  Developing a financial plan for securing sufficient revenues to cover the costs of implementing strategies

Transportation planning deals with planning of transportation facilities to meet present and future needs in sustainable manner e.g estimation of future demands, needs & problems, preparing plan for implementations. Transportation Planning

• Transportation planning is a process that leads to the decision on transportation policies and programs. • In other words a process to provide information necessary for making decision on when and where improvements should be in the transportation system, thus promoting travel and land development patterns that are in keeping with community goals and objectives. Transportation Planning

Transportation engineering or transport engineering is the application of technology and scientific principles to the planning, functional design, operation and management of facilities for any mode of transportation in order to provide for the safe, efficient, rapid, comfortable, convenient, economical, and environmentally compatible movement of people and goods. Transportation Engineering

• The basic purpose of the transportation is to provide efficient access to various activities that satisfy the human needs. • Thus general goal of the transportation is to accommodate these needs for mobility Whose mobility? for what purpose? by what means? at what cost? and to whom? Transportation Planning is about five important points: • Understanding of travel pattern in urban area What Transportation Planning is about?

• Understanding of causing factors that influence the demand for travel pattern • Development of relationship between travel pattern and causing factors • Application or use of this relationship to predict future demand for travel and to predict future travel pattern • Prediction of transport infrastructure requirement based on the predicted travel demand What Transportation Planning is about?

• Transportation planning is the process of defining future policies, goals, investments and designs to prepare for future needs to move people and goods to destinations. • “A collaborative and participatory process involving agencies, organizations and the public in a comprehensive look at national, state, regional and community needs…It examines demographic characteristics and travel patterns for a given area, shows how these characteristics will change over a given period of time and evaluates alternative improvements for the transportation system.“ • (Definition by Designing Walkable Urban Thoroughfares) What Transportation Planning is about?

• The planning aspects of transportation engineering relate to urban planning, and involve technical forecasting decisions and political factors. • Technical forecasting of passenger travel usually involves an urban transportation planning model, requiring the estimation of trip generation (how many trips for what purpose), trip distribution (destination choice, where is the traveler going), mode choice (what mode is being taken), and route assignment (which streets or routes are being used). Transportation Planning Aspects

• More sophisticated forecasting can include other aspects of traveler decisions, including auto ownership, trip chaining (the decision to link individual trips together in a tour) and the choice of residential or business location (known as land use forecasting). Passenger trips are the focus of transportation engineering because they often represent the peak of demand on any transportation system. • Requires accurate regional economic forecasts as well as accurate forecasts of highway users’ social and behavioral responses regarding trip-oriented decisions, in order to predict growth/decline trends and traffic diversion Transportation Planning Aspects

Transportation Planning Primary Purpose: To generate information useful to decision makers on the consequences of alternative transportation actions Decision Makers - $ Technical Limitation of Decision Maker Process of:  Understanding the types of decisions that need to be made  Assessing opportunities and limitations of the future  Identifying short and long-term consequences of alternative choices  Relating alternative decisions to the goals and objectives for the area  Presenting the information to decision makers in an understandable and useful form

Transportation Planning Transportation Planning Process :  How decisions to build transportation facilities are made  Evaluation and selection of highway or transit facilities to serve present and future land uses Factors commonly used to justify projects :  Improved traffic flow  Improved safety  Savings in energy consumption  Savings in travel time  Economic growth  Increased accessibility  Other reasons  Stimulate employment in a particular region  To compete with other cities /areas for prestige  To attract industry  To respond to political pressures

Projects may NOT be selected due to:  Opposition from those that would be adversely affected • A new highway that may require acquisition of residential property • A new airport that may cause excessive noise due to low flying planes Basic Elements: • Situation definition • To understand the situation that gave rise to the need for transportation improvement • Problem definition • To describe the problem and to identify quantifiable objectives • Search for solutions • To identify a variety of ideas, designs, locations, configurations that may provide solutions • Analysis of performance • To estimate how each of the proposed alternatives would perform under present and future conditions Transportation Planning

• A system is a group of interdependent and interrelated components that form a complex and unified system intended to serve some purpose through the performance of its interacting parts. • Understanding of the transportation system is very important to understand travel pattern and behavior of people in urban area. Transportation System

A transportation system may be defined as consisting of the fixed facilities, the flow entities, and the control system that permit people and goods to overcome the friction of geographical space (i.e. to move from one point to other) efficiently in order to participate in a timely manner in some desired activity. • Fixed Facilities • Flow Entities • Control System Transportation System

Fixed facilities: Fixed facilities are the physical component of the system that are fixed in space and constitute the network of links (e.g. roadways, rail tracks etc) and nodes (e.g. intersections, interchanges, transit terminals, airports etc) Transportation System
Flow entities: flow entities are the units that use the fixed facilities. They include all types of vehicles. Transportation System

Control system: The control system consists of vehicular control and flow control. Vehicular control: e.g. Manual control in vehicles Flow control: e.g. control of traffic on roads. Transportation System

Transportation System Classification 31 Modes of the System  Highways  Railways  Waterways  Airways  Pipelines The Components of the mode  The way  The vehicle  The Terminal  The control  The user Development of Components • Planning • Evaluation • Construction • Operation • Maintenance

Any transportation system consists of various modes of travel ranging from walking to driving to use crafts that fly. The classification of transportation system is to form classes of different modes of travel. Such classification is termed as modal classification. Modal Classification

 Mode: A mode of transport may be simply defined as means of transportation. A mode includes walking, bus, train, ferry boat, ship, aircraft, helicopter and so on.  1. Roadways  2. Railways  3. Airways  4. Waterways Modal Classification

ROADWAYS: All vehicles use roadways to travel from one point to other. Motorized vehicles: automobiles, trucks, buses etc Non-motorized vehicles: cycles, animal carts Types of Roads: 1. Expressways/Freeways 2. Arterials/state highways 3. Collectors/District roads 4. Local roads Modal classification

Expressways/Freeways: These are intercity roads with high speed of travel and with limited access. State Highways/ Arterials: These are intra city roads with high speed and controlled access. Collectors: These roads collects traffic from local and merge it into arterials. Locals: These roads have very good accessibility. These can be accessed by every home. But these roads offer very low speed. Modal classification

Important aspects of roadways are:  Safe and efficient operation  Control of road traffic  Layout of roads  Structural design of roads  Pavement design  Public transportation Modal classification

RAILWAYS: In this mode of travel all vehicles use rail track to move from one point to another.  Vehicles in this class consist of a long train of coaches attached to locomotive. This mode is used to transport people as well as goods. These are good for high speed mass transit.  The movement of trains on rail tracks is controlled through signal systems, operated either manually or automatically. Modal classification

Stations: Pre-specified locations where trains stop are known as stations. Following activities take place at stations:  Boarding and alignment of passengers  Loading and unloading of goods  Regrouping of coaches  Maintenance of activities  Ticketing Modal classification

Important aspects of railways are:  Safe and efficient operation  Control of rail traffic  Layout of rail tracks  Structural design of sub grade on which rail tracks run  Planning of stations Modal classification
WATERWAYS: In this form of transport all vehicles use channels in water bodies (like rivers, lakes, and oceans) to travel from one point to another. Modal classification
Important aspects of waterways are:  Safe and efficient operation  Control of ship traffic specially at and near ports  Planning and operation of ports Modal classification

AIRWAYS: In this mode of transport vehicles use air routes to travel from one point to another. Air routes are charted paths in the air based on various characteristics like directness of connections, prevailing atmospheric and wind connections, international agreements and safety issues, The activities at an airport are:  Boarding and alighting of passengers  Loading and unloading of cargo  Refueling  Maintenance  Air traffic control  Ticketing Modal classification

Important aspects of airways are:  Safe and efficient operation  Control of air traffic specially at and near airports  Planning and operation of airports  Orientation of runways  Planning and parking pattern of aircrafts  Structural design of runways, taxiways, and aprons  Planning and operation of vehicle circulation and parking Modal classification

A transportation system can be classified in terms of the basic elements which constitute any mode of transport. These are  Driver  Vehicle  Way  Control  Terminal  User Elemental classification

 Driver: Every mode of transportation have a driver who controls the vehicle used in that mode.  Vehicle: The vehicles used in the transportation have certain characteristics (for example: turning radius, braking distance, accelerating capabilities.  Way: Every mode of transportation uses a specified path which is either constructed or charted.  Control: in order to ensure the safety, there are controls which are imposed on the system. 1.1 Travel Demand Forecasting: Trends and Issues While there are other methods used to estimate travel demand in urban areas, travel demand forecasting and modeling remain important tools in the analysis of transportation plans, projects, and policies. Modeling results are useful to those making transportation decisions (and analysts assisting in the decision-making process) in system and facility design and operations and to those developing transportation policy.  The four-step modeling process has seen a number of enhancements. 1.2 Overview of the Four-Step Travel Modeling Process The methods presented in this report follow the conventional sequential process for estimating transportation demand that is often called the “four-step” process:  Step 1—Trip Generation (discussed in Section 4.4),  Step 2—Trip Distribution (discussed in Section 4.5),  Step 3—Mode Choice (discussed in Section 4.7), and  Step 4—Assignment (discussed in Sections 4.11 and 4.12). There are other components commonly included in the four-step process, as shown in Figure 1.1 and described in the following paragraphs. The serial nature of the process is not meant to imply that the decisions made by travelers are actually made sequentially rather than simultaneously, nor that the decisions are made in exactly the order implied by the four-step process. For example, the decision of the destination for the trip may follow or be made simultaneously with the choice of mode. Nor is the four-step process meant to imply that the decisions for each trip are made independently of the decisions for other trips. For example, the choice of a mode for a given trip may

with the choice of mode. Nor is the four-step process meant to imply that the decisions for each trip are made independently of the decisions for other trips. For example, the choice of a mode for a given trip may depend on the choice of mode in the preceding trip. In four-step travel models, the unit of travel is the “trip,” defined as a person or vehicle traveling from an origin to a destination with no intermediate stops. Since people traveling for different reasons behave differently, four-step models segment trips by trip purpose. The number and definition of trip purposes in a model depend on the types of information the model needs to provide for planning analyses, the

characteristics of the region being modeled, and the availability of data with which to obtain model parameters and the inputs to the model. The minimum number of trip purposes in most models is three: home-based work, home-based nonwork, and nonhome based. In this report, these three trip purposes are referred to as the “classic three” purposes. The purpose of trip generation is to estimate the number of trips of each type that begin or end in each location, based on the amount of activity in an analysis area. In most models, trips are aggregated to a specific unit of geography (e.g., a traffic analysis zone). The estimated number of daily trips will be in the flow unit that is used by the model, which is usually one of the following: vehicle trips; person trips in motorized modes (auto and transit); or person trips by all modes, including both motorized and nonmotorized (walking, bicycling) modes. Trip generation models require some explanatory variables that are related to trip- making behavior and some functions that estimate the number of trips based on these

or person trips by all modes, including both motorized and nonmotorized (walking, bicycling) modes. Trip generation models require some explanatory variables that are related to trip- making behavior and some functions that estimate the number of trips based on these explanatory variables. Typical variables include the number of households classified by characteristics such as number of persons, number of workers, vehicle availability, income level, and employment by type. The output of trip generation is trip productions and attractions by traffic analysis zone and by purpose. Trip distribution addresses the question of how many trips travel between units of geography (e.g., traffic analysis zones). In effect, it links the trip productions and attractions from the trip generation step. Trip distribution requires explanatory variables that are related to the cost (including time) of travel between zones, as well as the amount of trip-making activity in both the origin zone and the destination zone. Time-of-day modeling is used to divide the daily trips into trips for various time periods, such as morning and afternoon peak periods, mid-day, and evening. This division may occur at any point between trip generation and trip assignment. Most four-step models that include the time-of-day step use fixed factors applied to daily trips by purpose, although more sophisticated time-of-day choice models are sometimes used. While the four-step process focuses on personal travel, commercial vehicle/freight travel is a significant component of travel in most urban areas and must also be considered in the model. While simple factoring methods applied to personal travel trip tables are sometimes used, a better approach is to model such travel separately, creating truck/commercial vehicle trip tables. The final step in the four-step process is trip assignment. This step consists of separate highway and transit assignment processes. The highway assignment process routes vehicle trips from the origin-destination trip tables onto paths along the highway network, resulting in traffic volumes on network links by time of day and, perhaps, vehicle type. The highway assignment process routes vehicle trips from the origin-destination trip tables onto paths along the highway network, resulting in traffic volumes on network links by time of day and, perhaps, vehicle type. C H A P T E R 2 Planning Applications Context The purpose of developing travel forecasting models is to provide information that can be used to make transportation planning decisions. These decisions may require different kinds of information from the model, depending on the context. The planning context, therefore, should be used to determine the appropriate model structure, parameters, and complexity. This decision, in turn, will ensure that the travel forecasting model is appropriate for each planning context. It is useful to develop a travel forecasting model that meets most (if not all) of an agency’s current and future planning needs. This chapter discusses how the planning context affects the model’s capa-bilities and provides examples of different contexts found in U.S. urban areas. 1.1 Types of Planning Analyses The transportation planning function covers a diverse set of activities that focuses on different transportation modes and systems, timeframes, geographic scales, policy issues, and stakeholder groups. It is critical to gather input from a broad cross section of stakeholders on the types of policy considerations and modal analyses that need to

focuses on different transportation modes and systems, timeframes, geographic scales, policy issues, and stakeholder groups. It is critical to gather input from a broad cross section of stakeholders on the types of policy considerations and modal analyses that need to be accounted for in the travel demand model prior to its development. Many planning requirements are directed by federal legislation, such as long-range transportation planning and air quality planning. Federal guidelines and regulations regarding transportation planning are summarized by agency in Appendix A. Planning practices for these requirements are generally consistent across areas of the same

NCHRP Synthesis 311 (Shaw, 2003) and TCRP Report 88 (Kittelson and Associates et al., 2003) provide a starting point for understanding the development and application of performance measures. 1.1.2 Long-Range Transportation Planning Federal statutes require an MPO to prepare a long-range transportation plan (LRTP) and set forth many of the planning guidelines. Chief among these is a typical planning horizon of 20 to 30 years. This is not to say that other horizon years cannot be modeled, but the reliability of forecasts with a planning horizon of more than 30 years is highly questionable. 1.2 Overview of the Four-Step Travel Modeling Process The methods presented in this report follow the conventional sequential process for estimating transportation demand that is often called the “four-step” process:  Step 1—Trip Generation (discussed in Section 4.4),  Step 2—Trip Distribution (discussed in Section 4.5),  Step 3—Mode Choice (discussed in Section 4.7), and  Step 4—Assignment (discussed in Sections 4.11 and 4.12). There are other components commonly included in the four-step process, as shown in Figure 1.1 and described in the following paragraphs. The serial nature of the process is not meant to imply that the decisions made by travelers are actually made sequentially rather than simultaneously, nor that the decisions are made in exactly the order implied by the four-step process. For example, the decision of the destination for the trip may follow or be made simultaneously with the choice of mode. Nor is the four-step process meant to imply that the decisions for each trip are made independently of the decisions for other trips. For example, the choice of a mode for a given trip may

with the choice of mode. Nor is the four-step process meant to imply that the decisions for each trip are made independently of the decisions for other trips. For example, the choice of a mode for a given trip may depend on the choice of mode in the preceding trip. In four-step travel models, the unit of travel is the “trip,” defined as a person or vehicle traveling from an origin to a destination with no intermediate stops. Since people traveling for different reasons behave differently, four-step models segment trips by trip purpose. The number and definition of trip purposes in a model depend on the types of information the model needs to provide for planning analyses, the

characteristics of the region being modeled, and the availability of data with which to obtain model parameters and the inputs to the model. The minimum number of trip purposes in most models is three: home-based work, home-based nonwork, and nonhome based. In this report, these three trip purposes are referred to as the “classic three” purposes. The purpose of trip generation is to estimate the number of trips of each type that begin or end in each location, based on the amount of activity in an analysis area. In most models, trips are aggregated to a specific unit of geography (e.g., a traffic analysis zone). The estimated number of daily trips will be in the flow unit that is used by the model, which is usually one of the following: vehicle trips; person trips in motorized modes (auto and transit); or person trips by all modes, including both motorized and nonmotorized (walking, bicycling) modes. Trip generation models require some explanatory variables that are related to trip- making behavior and some functions that estimate the number of trips based on these explanatory variables. Typical variables include the number of households classified by characteristics such as number of persons, number of workers, vehicle availability, income level, and employment by type. The output of trip generation is trip productions and attractions by traffic analysis zone and by purpose. Trip distribution addresses the question of how many trips travel between units of geography (e.g., traffic analysis zones). In effect, it links the trip productions and attractions from the trip generation step. Trip distribution requires explanatory variables that are related to the cost (including time) of travel between zones, as well as the amount of trip-making activity in both the origin zone and the destination zone. Models of external travel estimate the trips that originate or are destined outside the model’s geographic region (the model area). These models include elements of trip generation and distribution, and so the outputs are trip tables represent-ing external travel. Mode choice is the third step in the four-step process. In this step, the trips in the tables output by the trip distribution step are split into trips by travel mode. The mode definitions vary depending on the types of transportation options offered in the model’s geographic region and the types of planning analyses required, but they can be generally grouped into automobile, transit, and nonmotorized modes. C H A P T E R 2 Planning Applications Context The purpose of developing travel forecasting models is to provide information that can be used to make transportation planning decisions. These decisions may require different kinds of information from the model, depending on the context. The planning context, therefore, should be used to determine the appropriate model structure, parameters, and complexity. This decision, in turn, will ensure that the travel forecasting model is appropriate for each planning context. It is useful to develop a travel forecasting model that meets most (if not all) of an agency’s current and future planning needs. This chapter discusses how the planning context affects the model’s capa-bilities and provides examples of different contexts found in U.S. urban areas. 1.1 Types of Planning Analyses The transportation planning function covers a diverse set of activities that focuses on different transportation modes and systems, timeframes, geographic scales, policy issues, and stakeholder groups. It is critical to gather input from a broad cross section of stakeholders on the types of policy considerations and modal analyses that need to

It is critical to gather input from a broad cross section of stakeholders on the types of policy considerations and modal analyses that need to be accounted for in the travel demand model prior to its development. Many planning requirements are directed by federal legislation, such as long-range transportation planning and air quality planning. Federal guidelines and regulations regarding transportation planning are summarized by agency in Appendix A. Planning practices for these requirements are generally consistent across areas of the same

TRANSPORTATION PLANNING AND ENGINEERING PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING transit systems, network design, bus service planning, capacity and operations

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING 1. What is public transportation planning? 3 • Transportation planning is a future-oriented process that supports decisions about policies, programmes and investments in the transport system. • It identifies when and where improvements are needed so that travel and land-use patterns support community goals. • Public transport planning focuses on moving people efficiently, safely and affordably—not simply moving vehicles. • Planning is iterative: understand existing conditions → forecast needs → assess alternatives → select a strategy → fund, implement and monitor.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING The urban transportation planning process 4 • Monitor existing conditions: population, employment, land use, travel patterns and network performance. • Forecast future population, employment and land-use growth; identify likely growth corridors. • Identify present and future transport problems and estimate travel demand. • Develop and compare alternative capital investments and operating strategies. • Assess environmental and wider impacts, including air quality, noise and land development. • Prepare a financial plan and implementation programme; monitor outcomes and update the plan.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Urban public transport demand patterns 5 Common trip patterns • Radial trips: between outer areas and the CBD. • Circumferential trips: around the city, linking suburbs or activity centres. • Local trips: within neighbourhoods or local districts. • CBD trips: movements within the central area. • Inter-centre trips: between major employment, education, health or commercial centres. What planners need to understand • Where trips begin and end (spatial pattern). • When trips occur (temporal pattern and peak periods). • How many people travel and in which direction. • Which destinations generate the strongest demand. • Whether demand is concentrated along corridors or dispersed.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING How are public transport systems classified? M.Sc. Transportation Engineering | TEM-403 7 • Transit modes can be classified using three main characteristics: • Right-of-way (ROW): degree of separation from other traffic. • Type of service: geographic scale and stopping pattern. • Technology: vehicle and propulsion/guideway system, such as bus, light rail or metro. • These dimensions should be considered together; a mode name alone does not describe its operating conditions.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Right-of-way classification 8 Category A — exclusive ROW • Fully controlled right-of-way with no legal access by other traffic. • Typically grade-separated and protected from road congestion. • Can support high speed, reliability and capacity. • Example: metro or rail on a fully separated alignment. Category B and C • Category B: physically separated longitudinally, but with at-grade crossings for vehicles or pedestrians. • Example: light rail crossing some streets at surface level. • Category C: transit operates in mixed traffic on ordinary streets. • Many conventional bus routes and streetcars operate in Category C.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Service types and families of transit modes 9 Service by geographic role • Short-haul: low-speed service within compact, high-density areas such as a CBD. • City transit: common urban service connecting neighbourhoods and city destinations. • Regional transit: longer-distance, higher-speed service with fewer stops; e.g. express bus or regional rail. Families of public transport • Street transit: regular buses, trolleybuses and streetcars/trams. • Semi-rapid transit: semi-rapid bus and light rail, depending on ROW and operation. • Rapid transit: metro/rail rapid transit • Paratransit: taxis, dial-a-ride, carpools and vanpools.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Paratransit: an intermediate service family 10 • Paratransit includes small passenger vehicles providing fare-paying or shared transport, often alongside conventional public transport. • It can serve as an alternative where fixed-route service is unavailable, infrequent or poorly matched to dispersed demand. • Examples: taxi, dial-a-ride, carpool and vanpool. • Spatial–temporal patterns: fixed space–variable time ; fixed time–variable space (carpool/vanpool); variable time–variable space (taxi and dial-a-ride).

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING 3. Key characteristics used to evaluate transit 11 • System performance: frequency, operating speed, reliability, safety, line capacity, productivity and utilization. • Level of service (LOS): an overall measure of service performance and quality as experienced by users. • Service impacts: short-run effects such as congestion, air pollution and noise; longer-run effects such as land values, economic activity and urban form. • Costs: capital/investment costs and operating costs. • Transit can become time- and cost-competitive with private vehicles when supported by dedicated lanes, exclusive ROW, signal priority and well-designed interchanges.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Transit performance: key terms 12 Measure | Meaning / interpretation Frequency (f) | Number of transit departures per hour. Headway (h) | Time interval between successive vehicles; for regular service, h = 60/f (minutes). Operating speed | Speed experienced by the passenger over the journey. Reliability | Consistency of service; e.g. proportion of arrivals within an agreed time window. Safety | May be expressed through crash/incident rates, such as accidents per million vehicle-km. Line capacity | Maximum number of people passing a point in a given time under stated conditions. Product capacity | Operating speed × line capacity (Vo × C) |

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Transit quality of service 13 Availability: can the trip be made? • Service exists near the origin. • Service exists near the destination. • Service operates when the passenger needs it. • Information is available on routes, stops, times and how to use the system. • Walking access to and from stops is feasible. Quality: how good is the trip? • Passenger loads and crowding. • Stop amenities and comfort of facilities. • Frequency, schedule adherence and reliability. • Door-to-door travel time compared with other modes. • Fare affordability and ease of payment. • Personal safety and security, including access walks and transfers.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING What makes public transport useful to passengers? 14 • It takes me where I want to go. • It takes me when I want to go. • It makes good use of my time. • It is good value for my money. • It treats me with respect and provides a safe, comfortable journey. • I can trust it to be reliable and it gives me flexibility to change my plans. • Planning implication: balance coverage, frequency, directness, affordability and passenger experience.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING 4. Route and network planning: basic concepts M.Sc. Transportation Engineering | TEM-403 15 • A route is an individual path followed by transit vehicles; a network is a system of connected routes. • A route has a spatial element (streets, stops and terminals) and a temporal element (service times and frequency). • Route structure should reflect the distribution of population, employment and major activity centres. • Three common structures are grid, radial and a combination of grid and radial networks.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Grid network structure 16 How it works • Routes run in broadly parallel north–south and east–west directions. • Passengers can reach many destinations with one transfer. • Works well where the street pattern and activity distribution support a grid. • Parallel route spacing is related to maximum acceptable walking distance. Planning strengths and constraints • Can reduce overlapping route mileage and allow higher frequency within a fixed budget. • Requires frequent service so transfer and waiting times remain low. • May require bus priority or exclusive lanes in congested central areas. • Less effective where street patterns are discontinuous or pedestrian access is poor.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Grid spacing and access 17 • In an ideal grid, a passenger is within walking distance of one north–south route and one east–west route. • The ideal spacing between parallel lines is approximately twice the maximum walking distance. • Illustrative local-bus example: if maximum walking distance is about 400 m, ideal parallel route spacing is about 800 m. • Actual spacing should reflect density, barriers, street connectivity, topography, safety and service frequency. Planning relationship Route spacing ≈ 2 × maximum acceptable walking distance

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Radial network structure 18 How it works • Routes radiate between the CBD and outer residential or suburban areas. • Well suited to cities where the CBD is the dominant employment and activity centre. • Can provide direct journeys for suburb-to-CBD commuters. • Radial routes may use bus lanes or other priority measures. Limitations • Suburb-to-suburb trips may require long detours or transfers. • Service converges on the CBD, potentially concentrating buses and congestion. • Efficiency weakens when activity centres are distributed rather than CBD-focused. • Circumferential routes can improve connections between outer areas.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Combined grid and radial networks 19 • Many cities combine radial routes for suburb-to-centre travel with a grid structure for movement within the central area. • The radial component connects outer residential areas with major centres. • The grid component provides cross-town movement and distributes passengers between local destinations. • The best network is context-specific: respond to trip patterns, street geometry, density and activity centres. • Do not assume that one network form is universally best.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Direct service versus a connecting network 20 Direct-service example • One direct route runs every 30 minutes. • Average waiting time = 30/2 = 15 minutes. • In-vehicle travel time = 20 minutes. • Average journey time = 15 + 20 = 35 minutes. • Advantage: no transfer is required. Connecting-service example • Two connecting legs each run every 10 minutes. • Average first wait = 5 minutes; first ride = 10 minutes. • Average transfer wait = 5 minutes; second ride = 10 minutes. • Average journey time = 5 + 10 + 5 + 10 = 30 minutes. • Higher frequency can reduce total journey time despite a transfer.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING The transfer trade-off: frequency versus directness 21 • A connective network can provide higher frequencies for the same total budget by reducing route duplication and overlapping mileage. • Higher frequency reduces average waiting time and can improve average travel time and ridership. • Transfers impose a penalty: walking between services, uncertainty, waiting, accessibility barriers and perceived inconvenience. • Network design must balance direct journeys against frequency, coverage, transfer quality and total door-to-door time.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING 5. Main elements of bus service planning 22 • A. Evaluate demand: estimate the number, location and timing of potential passengers. • B. Design route and network structure: select corridors, stops, terminals and connections. • C. Design fare structure and payment options. • D. Undertake preliminary schedule design: estimate running time, cycle time, headway and fleet. • E. Complete final schedule design and vehicle blocking. • These stages are interdependent and should be revisited when demand, resources or operating conditions change.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING A. Evaluation of bus service demand 23 • Estimate how many people may use the proposed route instead of their current travel mode. • Use existing traffic and public transport data, origin–destination information and focused surveys. • Identify peak periods, dominant travel directions and major trip generators such as schools, hospitals, shopping centres and employment areas. • Examine spatial demand (where trips occur) and temporal demand (when trips occur). • Travel-demand forecasting can use trip generation, trip distribution and mode-choice/mode-split analysis to estimate potential ridership.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING B. Fare structure and payment options 24 Fare structures • Uniform fare: simple to understand and administer, but short-distance passengers may pay relatively more per kilometre. • Distance-based fare: more closely reflects distance travelled, but can be complex to calculate and administer. • Zone-based fare: passengers pay according to the zones crossed; a compromise between simplicity and distance equity. Fare collection methods • Driver collection: straightforward but can increase boarding delays. • On-board or stop-based fare machines: reduce the driver's role in payment and can speed boarding. • Fare cards / smart cards: faster boarding and can record route, stop and time information for planning and monitoring.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING C. Preliminary schedule design: worked example 25 Given: a route links a residential neighbourhood and the CBD. Input | Value One-way route distance | 5 miles Average operating speed | 12 miles/hour Desired service headway (initial target) | 15 minutes Peak-point forecast demand | 400 passengers/hour One-way running time Time = distance ÷ speed = 5 ÷ 12 hour = 25 minutes Round-trip running time 2 × 25 = 50 minutes (before layover / recovery) The fleet requirement must use the full cycle time, not just the one-way running time. Allow time at terminals for recovery, schedule regulation and driver needs.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Fleet requirement, cycle time and headway M.Sc. Transportation Engineering | TEM-403 26 • Cycle time (C) = round-trip travel time + layover/recovery time. • Example: 50 minutes running time + 10 minutes total recovery/layover = 60-minute cycle time. • Fleet required (N) = cycle time ÷ desired headway. • At a 15-minute headway: N = 60/15 = 4 vehicles, before any additional operational reserve. Capacity = vehicles/hour x passengers/vehicle =4 x 75 = 300 (revise number of vehicles based on headway) • If demand/capacity requires a 10-minute headway: N = 60/10 = 6 vehicles. Capacity = 6 x 75 = 450 • Headway and fleet size must be checked against service objectives and passenger demand.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Operational terms used in capacity and scheduling 27 • Headway: time between consecutive buses arriving at a stop or terminal. • Dwell time: time a vehicle remains stopped to serve passengers, including door opening/closing and boarding/alighting. • Clearance time: time losses at a stop other than passenger dwell time • Passenger load: number of passengers on board; load factor relates occupancy to available seating capacity. • Layover/recovery: scheduled time at a terminal between trips, used to absorb delays and support driver breaks or changeovers. • Terminal points: route ends; intermediate time points are selected at major trip generators and interchange locations.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING 6. Transit capacity: people as well as vehicles 28 • Transit capacity differs from highway capacity because it measures the movement of both vehicles and passengers. • Vehicle-carrying capacity: maximum number of vehicles that can pass a point during a specified period. • Passenger-carrying capacity: maximum number of people that can pass a point during a specified period under stated operating conditions. • At a simple level: passenger capacity per hour = vehicles per hour × passengers per vehicle. • Capacity depends on vehicle size, occupancy, service frequency/headway, dwell time, stop and platform arrangements, and available movement channels. • Capacity is not a fixed property of the vehicle alone; it is a property of the whole operating system.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Basic capacity relationships 29 Service frequency f = 60 / h f = vehicles per hour; h = headway in minutes. Passenger line capacity Cp = f × S S = average passengers per vehicle.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Factors influencing transit line capacity 30 • Vehicle characteristics: vehicle size, door arrangement, passenger space and loading capability. • Right-of-way characteristics: exclusive, partially separated or mixed traffic. • Stop characteristics: stop spacing, loading positions, platform capacity and passenger circulation. • Operating characteristics: speed, dwell time, clearance time and service regularity. • Passenger traffic characteristics: boarding/alighting volumes, passenger distribution and load factor. • Street traffic characteristics and signal control, including green-time allocation. • Headway control and operating variability; analytical estimates should be checked against actual operating experience.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING D. Final schedule design and vehicle blocking 32 • Preliminary scheduling establishes the required frequency, cycle time and number of vehicles. • Final schedule design assigns departure, arrival and departure-again times at both terminals and selected intermediate time points. • Layover/recovery time is included so vehicles can absorb delays and begin the next trip reliably. • Vehicle blocking links successive trips into a sequence that can be operated by one vehicle. • A block may include multiple trips and may include more than one route during a vehicle's working day.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Vehicle blocking: assigning trips to vehicles 34 With a 60-minute cycle and a 10-minute headway, six vehicles are required. Block | Leave A | Arrive B | Leave B | Arrive A Vehicle 1 | 07:00 | 07:25 | 07:30 | 07:55 Vehicle 2 | 07:10 | 07:35 | 07:40 | 08:05 Vehicle 3 | 07:20 | 07:45 | 07:50 | 08:15 Vehicle 4 | 07:30 | 07:55 | 08:00 | 08:25 Vehicle 5 | 07:40 | 08:05 | 08:10 | 08:35 Vehicle 6 | 07:50 | 08:15 | 08:20 | 08:45 What blocking achieves It links trips into workable vehicle duties, supports fleet planning and helps estimate vehicle operating costs and operator work assignments.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING 7. Service impacts and planning evaluation 35 Potential short-run impacts • Changes in road congestion and delay. • Changes in air pollution and energy use. • Noise, visual quality and street environment. • Passenger access and interchange conditions. Potential long-run impacts • Changes in land values and development patterns. • Changes in economic activity and access to jobs/services. • Changes in urban form and density around corridors. • Changes in the social environment and mobility opportunities.

PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION PLANNING Class discussion and application 38 Numerical / design exercise • A bus route has a 40-minute round-trip running time and 8 minutes of terminal recovery. • Calculate the fleet required for a 12-minute headway. • If each bus carries 60 passengers and operates 5 trips per hour past a point, estimate simple passenger capacity per hour. • Identify two operational factors that could reduce practical capacity.

Types of Bus Stop Placement There are three main locations for placing bus stops near intersections. Far-side bus stop Located immediately after an intersection. Advantages: Reduces conflicts with left-turning vehicles. Allows passengers to cross behind the bus. Disadvantages: Bus may block the intersection. Can reduce visibility. May increase rear-end collision risk. Suitable for: Intersections with heavy turning movements

Near-side bus stop Located immediately before an intersection. Advantages: Convenient access to the crosswalk. Passengers can board while the traffic signal is red. May eliminate the need for a second stop. Disadvantages: Can conflict with left-turning vehicles. May obstruct traffic signals and pedestrian visibility. Can block through traffic. Suitable for: Locations where far-side placement is unsuitable.

Mid-block bus stop Located between two intersections. Advantages: Avoids some intersection-related conflicts. Can reduce pedestrian congestion at intersections. Disadvantages: May encourage unsafe road crossing. Can increase walking distance. Suitable for: Locations with major passenger generators between intersections.

Types of Bus Stop Zone Designs A bus stop zone is the section of road where a bus stops for passenger boarding and alighting. A. Curbside bus stop The bus stops directly alongside the road kerb. Advantages: Low construction cost, simple design and easy relocation. Disadvantages: Can obstruct traffic, create queues and encourage unsafe lane changes. Suitable for: Roads with speeds below 40 mph and adequate curb clearance. B. Bus bulb (curb extension or nub) The sidewalk is extended into the parking lane so the bus can stop without leaving the traffic lane. Advantages: Reduces the need to remove parking spaces. Shortens pedestrian crossing distance. Provides more passenger waiting space. Reduces bus delay when re-entering traffic. Disadvantage: Higher installation cost than a simple curbside stop. Suitable for: Streets where parking is important or curb space is limited.

C. Bus bay (turnout or berth) A separate space is provided beside the traffic lane for buses to stop. Advantages: Separates stopped buses from moving traffic. Reduces delays to through traffic. Disadvantages: Expensive construction. Difficult for buses to re-enter traffic. Difficult to relocate. Suitable for: Higher-speed roads (over 40 mph), long peak dwell times (over 30 seconds), layover requirements or multiple buses. D. Open bus bay A bus bay arrangement that allows buses to decelerate through an intersection into the stopping area. Its general advantages and disadvantages are similar to those of a conventional bus bay. E. Queue-jumper bus bay A special bus bay arrangement that allows buses to bypass traffic queues, often with signal assistance. Advantage: Reduces bus delays at congested intersections. Disadvantage: May delay right-turning vehicles and shares some disadvantages of conventional bus bays.

Regression Analysis • Regression analysis is study of relationship between one variable Y, called the dependent variable, and (several) others Xi, called the independent variables.

Regression Analysis and Transportation • To estimate ridership levels of public transportation • To estimate traffic management system performance • To predict crashes on interchange and non-interchange segments of roads • To forecast travel demand • To develop integrated land use models

Types of Regression Linear regression produces the slope of a line that best fits a single set of data. Multiple regression is the analysis of more than one set of data, which often produces a more realistic projection.

Simple Linear Regression Analysis  Assume that observations of the magnitude of a dependent variable Y have been obtained for n magnitudes of an independent variable X.  An equation of the form  Ye = a + bX  is to be fitted to the data. Where,  Ye = predicted scores (estimated values) of the dependent variable, Y  a = intercept constant  b = regression coefficient

Objectives of Regression Analysis  The primary goal is to determine the best set of parameters bi=n, such that the model predicts experimental values of the dependent variable as accurately as possible (i.e. calculated values ye should be close to experimental values y).

Accuracy and Validity of Regression Model There are many pieces of information in the Excel regression output but the following four items will give a quick read on the validity of the model. 1) Overall Regression Equation’s Accuracy (R Square and Adjusted R Square) 2) Probability That This Output Was Not By Chance (ANOVA – Significance of F) 3) Individual Regression Coefficient and Y-Intercept Accuracy 4) Visual Analysis of Residuals

(1) Overall Regression’s Accuracy • R2 – It is the ratio of the sum of squares explained by the regression to the total sum of squares, and is known as the coefficient of determination, and is usually denoted by the symbol, R2. • It is the most important number of the output. R2 informs how well the regression line approximates the real data. This number tells you how much of the output variable’s variance is explained by the input variables’ variance. • The value of R2 is given as

Ratio of Sum of Squares ∑y2 = ∑yd 2 + ∑ye 2 Where, ∑y2 = total sum of squares of the deviations of the Y observations about the mean value. ∑yd 2 = sum of squares of the deviations of the Y observations from the regression line Small ∑yd 2 considered to fit data well ∑ye 2 = the sum of squares of the deviations of the estimated value of Y (Ye) about the mean value.

Explanation of R2  The ratio R2 may assume a magnitude b/w 0 and 1.  For a regression for which R2 = 1, no variation  When R2 = 0, no relationship  Ideally, the value should be at least 0.6 (60%) or 0.7 (70%).  The square root of the coefficient of determination is termed as correlation coefficient.

2 & 3) F value and P value  Significance of F – This indicates the significance of the model.  P-value of each coefficient and the Y-intercept. This indicates the importance and significant of each variable in the model.

4) Visual Analysis of Residuals • The residuals are the difference between the Regression’s predicted value and the actual value of the output variable. • You can quickly plot the Residuals on a scatterplot chart. Look for patterns in the scatterplot.
